Purls of wisdom
A little yarn. A lot of math.

Purls of
wisdom

The surprisingly mathematical business of making a sweater fit.

Opening · 45 seconds“Have you ever made something exactly as instructed and discovered it fits someone else?” Pause for a show of hands. This talk follows one idea: measurements become counts, and counts become a shape. Point to the sweater: a 40-inch circumference at five stitches per inch needs 200 stitches around the body. The 20-inch flat width is half the circumference. This seamless-body example ignores stitch-pattern constraints. The numbers are teaching examples, not a complete garment pattern.
40 in × 5 st/in
= 200 stitches
01 / The fabric itself

A loop
through
a loop

Knitting builds fabric from connected loops of yarn. A new loop passes through an existing loop, and the needles hold the live loops while you work.

In a simple swatch, stitches sit beside one another in rows and stack into columns. That gives us two directions to count.

Knitting basics · 1 minuteUse the recreated loop diagram to show that the apparent grid comes from linked yarn loops. Each stitch connects with neighboring stitches, and the new row passes through loops from the row below. The live loops remain on the needle until worked or secured. The lower diagram overlays a grid on the same structure. Highlight a horizontal row, then a vertical column. Textile terminology calls these courses and wales. For the plain knitting in this talk, counting stitches across and rows upward gives us the two measurements used in gauge. The diagram is schematic and its square grid does not imply that real stitches are square. Loop geometry contributes to stretch, but fiber, yarn construction, stitch pattern and finishing also matter. Diagram recreated as editable vector paths from the presenter’s visual reference. Structure reference: NPTEL, Introduction and basic concepts of knitting. Loop shape lets knitted fabric change shape under tension. Yarn and stitch structure affect how much it stretches.

Linked loops become a fabric we can count.A row runs across the fabric. Stitches across determine width.A column stacks upward. Rows worked determine height.

02 / The conversion factor

Gauge is
a ratio

Stitch gauge converts stitches into width. Row gauge converts rows into length.

Stitches ÷ stitch gauge = width
Rows ÷ row gauge = length
Gauge · 1 minuteThe swatch always contains 20 columns and 28 rows. At the defaults, 5 stitches and 7 rows per inch, it measures 4 by 4 inches. Each gauge slider changes only its corresponding physical dimension. Both directions use the same fixed scale for inches. Higher stitch gauge makes a narrower swatch; higher row gauge makes it shorter. Gauge changes do not change the stitch or row counts. Measure in the intended stitch pattern after washing and blocking the swatch as you will the garment.
03 / Gauge and finished size

Same count.
New gauge.
Surprise size.

A body has 200 stitches around. The pattern expects 5 st/in. Your washed swatch gives 4 st/in.

Will the sweater be
smaller, the same, or larger?

Audience check · 1 minuteReveal the result after explaining the two gauges. At five stitches per inch, 200 stitches span 40 inches. At four stitches per inch they span 50 inches. The width factor is 5/4 = 1.25. This is a 25% circumference increase, not a claim that every dimension or the yarn requirement also increases 25%. To retain 40 inches at the new gauge, the arithmetic target is 160 stitches, subject to pattern and construction constraints. Pattern repeats and seam allowances can constrain your final stitch count. Recalculate lengths separately with row gauge.
200 stitches

Same stitches. Different footprint.

04 / Room to be yourself

The body.
The sweater.
The difference.

Ease is garment circumference minus body circumference. Positive ease gives extra room. Negative ease relies on fabric stretch.

Body + ease = garment
Ease · 1 minuteThe body stays at 36 inches. Move from negative to positive ease. Ask which fit the audience prefers. Fit depends on fabric, construction and preference, so the picture is a schematic, not a prediction of drape. Here the stitch count represents a seamless body circumference with no seam allowance. 5 st/in · Body worked in the round
05 / Stitch proportions

A stitch is
usually not
a square

Width uses stitch gauge. Height uses row gauge. A diagonal on graph paper can have a different angle in the fabric.

5 st/in   ≠   7 rows/in
Two gauges · 1 minuteToggle between chart squares and fabric proportions. Both diagrams contain ten columns and ten rows. At five stitches and seven rows per inch, a stitch is 0.2 inches wide and a row is about 0.143 inches high. The red diagonal moves one stitch horizontally per row vertically. Its physical sideways-per-upward ratio is 7/5, not 1.
06 / Shaping is a rate of change

Shaping
is slope

Waists, necklines, shoulders, sleeves: shaping gives fabric its angles and curves. Increases and decreases change width. Short rows change height.

For increases and decreases:
stitch change ÷ rows worked
Slope · 1½ minutesShaping creates angles and curves throughout a garment: waist shaping, neck openings, shoulders, armholes and sleeves. For an edge shaped with increases or decreases, this graph plots stitch change against rows worked. One stitch added every six rows gives +1/6 stitch per row at that edge; one removed gives −1/6. The direction follows the order of working, so reversing the knitting direction reverses the sign for the same garment edge. More frequent changes produce a larger absolute stitch-per-row rate. The solid line is whole-stitch steps; the dashed line is the average rate. Curves come from changing that local rate. Short-row shaping is the complementary case: extra rows create height differences across a width of stitches, so shoulder slope is often expressed as a row difference over a stitch span. This slide introduces the general idea; the graph demonstrates an increase/decrease edge.
07 / A sleeve, calculated

A pattern
hiding in
the numbers

Start at a 14-inch upper arm: 70 stitches at 5 st/in. A narrower cuff needs more decreases. A longer sleeve gives you more rounds to spread them out.

30 stitches removed ÷ 2
= 15 decrease rounds

Each decrease round removes two stitches. Change the cuff width or the number of rounds to change their spacing.

Sleeve lab · 1½ minutesChange either the width target or the shaping length. Row gauge stays fixed at 7 rounds per inch, so changing the number of rounds changes physical length. The top-down sleeve is shown opened flat. Hold the upper arm at 14 inches or 70 stitches, stitch gauge at 5 st/in, row gauge at 7 rounds/in, and start the shaping section at 90 rounds, about 12.9 inches. The length slider spans 30–120 rounds. Cuff targets are 8, 10 and 12 inches: respectively 40, 50 and 60 stitches. These require 30, 20 or 10 stitches removed, hence 15, 10 or 5 paired decrease rounds. Over 90 rounds, decrease every 6th, 9th or 18th round. Each interval includes the decrease round. At the default 8-inch cuff, work five rounds plain, then remove two stitches on the sixth round; repeat 15 times. The upper-arm width stays fixed. The cuff slider changes the lower width, and the shaping-length slider changes the height. When the round count is not divisible by the decrease count, use a mixture of adjacent whole-round intervals. Decrease round i occurs at floor(i × total rounds ÷ number of decrease rounds), so all decreases land on whole rounds, the last one lands on the last shaping round, and intervals differ by at most one round. The section excludes cuff ribbing, underarm pickup details and reserved plain rounds. These are arithmetic examples, not recommendations for an individual cuff fit.
08 / Raglan shaping

A slope
can change
as you go

Raglan lines separate the body and sleeves. A constant shaping rate makes a straight diagonal. Compound raglan shaping varies the rate through the yoke, or between body and sleeves.

That gives the shoulders, chest, and upper arms room to grow at different rates, so the contour can better match the intended fit.

Same totals.
Different contour.
Compound raglan · 1½ minutesFollow the orange line from neck to underarm. In the constant-rate example, one body edge gains one stitch every second round for 64 rounds, adding 32 stitches. In the compound example, the first 16 rounds add one stitch per round, the next 32 rounds add one every fourth round, and the final 16 rounds add one every second round. That is 16 + 8 + 8 = 32 stitches at the same edge over the same 64 rounds. Every schedule interval includes the increase round. The schematic plots cumulative widening against rounds; whole-stitch steps are simplified into straight segments. Both examples therefore reach the same endpoint, but distribute the fabric differently between neck and underarm. Dashed lines retain the constant-rate reference. Actual compound raglans can also give sleeve and body edges different schedules. This simplified illustration isolates one body edge; it is not a full yoke recipe and does not prescribe the increase schedule for every wearer. A constant-rate raglan can fit well; compound shaping gives a designer more control when a different contour is needed. Gauge, neck shaping, underarm stitches and fit checks still matter. Sources: Aimee Sher, compound raglan construction; Ailbíona McLochlainn, What Is a Compound Raglan?
09 / Sweater constructions

Where the
slopes live

Constructions · 1½ minutesSaddle shoulder: a narrow panel extends from the neckline across the top of the shoulder and continues into the sleeve. Shaping around that strip develops the body and sleeve cap. Lakes is the saddle-shoulder photo example. Theo uses picked-up sleeves with short-row sleeve caps. Bloodroot uses simultaneous set-in sleeve shaping; its description does not identify it as Susie Myers’s Contiguous method. Each card flips to its photo. The Contiguous card shows Bloodroot as a related simultaneous set-in example, rather than a confirmed use of Susie Myers’s method. Photo sources: Wednesday Sweater; Movement Tee; Theo; Bloodroot; Lakes. These are schematic examples of shaping geometry, not pattern schematics with measured angles. Orange marks the principal shaping paths; contiguous uses orange for the shoulder phase and green for the sleeve-cap phase. Wednesday Sweater by PetiteKnit is the drop-shoulder photo example: its shoulders are shaped with short rows, and sleeves are picked up around the armholes and worked toward the cuffs. Drop shoulder: the sleeve joins a wide body beyond the natural shoulder, often with a relatively straight armhole. Shoulder slope can be added using short rows or other shaping, but some drop-shoulder designs are simple rectangles with no shoulder slope. The sleeve commonly tapers toward the cuff. The raglan photo is Movement Tee by Lily Kate France. Its pattern uses compound raglan shaping; the eyelet line shows the path from neck to underarm. Raglan: lines of increases or decreases run from neckline to underarm, dividing body and sleeves. Constant or varying rates determine their trajectory. Set-in sleeve: the shaped sleeve cap fits a shaped armhole, while shoulder slope is a separate calculation. These pieces may be seamed or made using a seamless method. Contiguous: Susie Myers’s top-down method builds shoulder shaping first, then develops sleeve caps within continuous rows or rounds. It produces a set-in-like silhouette, so its final outline can resemble the set-in example; the distinction here is how and when the shaping is built. Highlighted paths can represent edges, join lines or shaping locations; they do not all represent seams or one-to-one stitch-increase tracks. Shoulder slope can involve changing the number of rows across width, as with short rows, whereas sleeve taper commonly changes stitches over rows. Sources: Susie Myers, Contiguous; Leslie Gonzalez, TKGA, shoulder shaping; The Knitting Architect; Tin Can Knits, raglan construction.
10 / Grading a pattern

Grading
the whole
garment

Pattern grading develops a design across sizes. Each measurement needs its own plan: a larger chest doesn’t mean a neckline or sleeve length grows by the same percentage.

Designers set targets for the chest, neckline, shoulders, and arms, then recalculate stitch counts and shaping rates to preserve the intended fit.

Pattern grading · 1½ minutesGrading is a set of related calculations, rather than one enlargement percentage. Neck circumference, shoulder width, chest circumference, upper-arm circumference and sleeve length need their own targets. First show the reference size, then scale every dimension by the chest ratio, 56/44. The body gets the intended circumference, but this also changes a 20-inch neckline to about 25.5 inches and a 24-inch body to about 30.5 inches. Finally show the independently chosen targets: 56-inch chest, 21-inch neck opening, 25-inch body, and 19-inch cross-back. All of these are invented finished garment measurements for this example, not claims about particular bodies or size labels. Neck opening circumference is the schematic neckline curve, not its straight width. At 5 st/in, the chest target adds 60 stitches while the neckline adds only 5 nominal stitches. Neckband gauge, ribbing stretch, stitch repeats and construction determine the actual neckline count. Designers also check upper-arm dimensions, armhole depth, shoulder placement, ease and fit across sizes, using measurements and fit feedback. A grading chart describes a size system, not every individual. Illustrative garment measurements. Body proportions vary within every size.

11 / Wearable math

You can
wear
the math

Loops give us rows and columns. Gauge gives the scale. Ease sets the target. Shaping rates connect the measurements, and those rates can change along the way.

Ratios and slopes do a lot of the work. Grading gives each measurement its own plan. Fabric stretch, drape, and construction finish the story.

Closing · 45 secondsReturn to the opening show of hands. “The next time a pattern says ‘increase every sixth round,’ you can read the shape behind the instruction.” Invite people to bring a garment they love, measure it, and compare those dimensions with a blocked swatch. These are arithmetic tools for understanding fit, not a substitute for a complete tested pattern. All numerical examples are illustrative calculations. Schematic visuals simplify fabric behavior.
inches × gauge = stitches
change ÷ length = rate
yarn + you = possibility
